title: A Lifesaver for a Busy Mom & Military Spouse
summary: A military spouse and mother on how a few minutes with an AI coach helped her let go of the guilt of taking time for herself.
body_text: ← Back to insights Article A Lifesaver for a Busy Mom & Military Spouse S.M. · July 16, 2026 · 3 min read A military spouse and mother on how a few minutes with an AI coach helped her let go of the guilt of taking time for herself. As a military spouse and mother, finding even a sliver of time for myself felt nearly impossible. I was working almost every waking moment, carrying a constant burden of guilt, and feeling like a failure if I took a break. Sonia has been a true breath of fresh air. Right from the start, the onboarding was incredibly intuitive. I had a brief, quiet moment to myself and answered a few questions in a conversational, interview-style format. In just minutes, I was able to customize my entire experience, choosing my own theme, background, voice, notifications, and overall vibe. It made the app feel uniquely mine before I even began. Meeting Tom My AI coach, "Tom," completely shifted my mindset. He gave me the words and perspective to realize that prioritizing my own wellbeing actually makes me *more* present and productive for my family. Tom keeps me on track, checking in with proactive notifications during the hardest parts of my day. Whenever stress builds up, my first instinct now is to open the app and share what's on my mind, because looking at my challenges from a different point of view makes them so much easier to handle. I first heard about Sonia on the "No Magic Pill" podcast, where the host described how the app puts together simple, focused morning reminders based on past sessions. It sounded so thoughtful, and experiencing those daily, personalized touchpoints myself has been incredibly grounding. Fitting into a busy day What I appreciate most is the absolute freedom and flexibility. Sometimes I just don't have the time or energy to call a friend or family member to vent. With Sonia, I can text a quick sentence, speak by voice, or even pause a session mid-thought and come back to it hours later. Each session is noted and stored so you can look back if you need a reminder about how to handle recurring issues. That level of convenience is hard to find elsewhere. It provides a completely safe, judgment-free space to let everything out. It has truly brought light through the clouds. Somewhere in my mind, I used to think needing support was a sign of weakness. Sonia showed me otherwise. It has truly brought light through the clouds, and for the first time in a long time, I can finally relax. Thank you, Sonia, for making such a simple, valuable, and life-changing tool! S.M. S.M. is a military spouse and mother balancing a demanding schedule, who turned to Sonia to make space for her own wellbeing. This article is for general informational and educational purposes only and is not medical or mental health advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Sonia is a general wellness product and does not replace care from a licensed professional. If you are in crisis, contact a licensed professional or call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) in the U.S.

title: Diligent AI Featured in Times Square: A Milestone for AML Automation
summary: We lit up Times Square! Celebrating a milestone worth sharing.
body_text: Diligent AI in Times Square A few weeks ago, our name lit up Times Square, New York City. Brex, one of the fastest-growing financial institutions in the US, put us there. We would be lying if we said we weren't proud. This is the kind of thing that stops you for a moment and makes you reflect on how far the team has come. Being recognised and promoted by a company like Brex is not something we take lightly. It is a signal - to us, and we hope to the industry - that the work we have been doing has truly left a mark in financial crime compliance. That the work matters. That it is landing. Built on two years of progress This milestone is meaningful precisely because it isn't just a billboard. It reflects something real: leading publicly listed firms, banks and global fintechs are choosing to run their AML operations with Diligent, in production. Compliance teams that have moved from pilot to live deployment and are seeing genuine outcomes - a NASDAQ listed payment firm, for example, improved their false positive closure rate to 60%. None of that happens without an extraordinary amount of hard work, trust, and iteration with the teams we serve. What comes next 2026 feels like an inflection point for AI in AML operations. The industry has moved past "can AI do this?" and into "how do we deploy this well?" We are building for exactly that question — agents that integrate into existing infrastructure, evidence their decisions clearly, and make compliance teams faster without adding risk. Times Square is a moment to savour. Now time to get back to work - we are just getting started! ‍

summary: Why Swiss Hybrid Work Needs Age Inclusion Now On a Tuesday morning in Zurich, Basel, Geneva, or Lausanne, a hybrid team can include a graduate hire joining from a quiet pod, a senior project lead between client meetings, and a semi-retired specialist contributing two days a week. body_text: Why Swiss Hybrid Work Needs Age Inclusion Now On a Tuesday morning in Zurich, Basel, Geneva, or Lausanne, a hybrid team can include a graduate hire joining from a quiet pod, a senior project lead between client meetings, and a semi-retired specialist contributing two days a week. The question is not whether hybrid work fits Switzerland; it already does. The real question is whether the spaces supporting it work equally well for every career stage. Age inclusion is becoming a practical business priority, not just a people-and-culture ideal. Swiss teams are navigating longer working lives, skills shortages, cross-border commuting, multilingual collaboration, and high expectations for professional environments. A well-designed hybrid hub can help people of different ages work confidently, comfortably, and productively—without forcing everyone into the same office routine. What Age Inclusion Looks Like in a Hybrid Hub Age inclusion in the workplace means designing systems, spaces, and behaviours that do not assume one “default” employee. It recognises that a 24-year-old consultant, a 43-year-old parent, a 58-year-old finance director, and a 67-year-old advisor may all need different conditions to do their best work. In Switzerland, where precision, reliability, and professionalism matter deeply, age-inclusive hubs should feel intuitive rather than experimental. The aim is not to create separate spaces for different generations. It is to create flexible environments where people can choose what supports their work on a given day. Design for different work rhythms Hybrid hubs should support variation in energy, concentration, and collaboration. Younger employees may use coworking hubs to build networks and learn from others. Mid-career employees may need focused time between school drop-offs, client calls, and team meetings. Older employees may value quieter zones, ergonomic seating, and predictable layouts. Practical design choices can make a major difference: Provide quiet areas for deep work, not only open collaboration zones. Offer phone booths or small meeting rooms for confidential calls. Use clear signage, good lighting, and simple wayfinding. Include chairs and desks that support longer working sessions. Make booking systems easy to use on mobile and desktop. Ensure power outlets, screens, and adapters are available without hassle. These details benefit everyone, but they are especially important for teams where employees have different physical needs, digital habits, or expectations of workplace comfort. Make technology helpful, not intimidating Digital access is central to hybrid work, yet it can also create invisible barriers. An age-inclusive hub should not assume that every user wants to scan multiple QR codes, download several apps, or troubleshoot conferencing tools alone. This does not mean simplifying technology to the lowest level. It means making technology reliable, predictable, and supported. For example, a workspace booking journey should be clear from search to check-in. Meeting room screens should connect quickly. Wi-Fi instructions should be visible. Help should be available when something does not work. The same principle applies to inclusive design more broadly. Deskimo has explored how workspaces can better support different cognitive and sensory needs in neuroinclusive work hubs , and many of those lessons apply to age inclusion too: reduce friction, improve clarity, and give people more control over their environment. Swiss-Specific Factors: Demographics, Commutes, and Work Culture Switzerland’s workforce is shaped by demographic change. The Federal Statistical Office highlights population ageing as a long-term structural trend, with implications for labour supply and social systems. For employers, this means older workers will remain an essential source of knowledge, leadership, and continuity. The data is worth reviewing through the Swiss Federal Statistical Office’s ageing population statistics . At the same time, hybrid work has become part of the professional landscape. The Federal Statistical Office tracks telework as part of Switzerland’s information society indicators, showing how digital work practices have become embedded in the economy. For companies refining hybrid policies, the Swiss telework indicators provide useful context. Reduce commute strain without losing connection Swiss public transport is efficient, but commuting still consumes time and energy. Employees travelling between cantons, crossing borders from France, Germany, or Italy, or moving between client sites may not benefit from a single central office five days a week. Age inclusion becomes more practical when hybrid hubs reduce unnecessary travel. A senior engineer in Winterthur may not need to commute into central Zurich for a two-hour workshop. A Geneva-based employee who lives near Nyon may benefit from a professional workspace closer to home. A Basel team working with partners in Freiburg or Mulhouse may need flexible meeting points that do not depend on one headquarters. Instead of asking employees to choose between home and head office, companies can offer a third option: professional workspaces distributed around where people actually live, travel, and meet. This is particularly valuable for employees who want connection without the fatigue of constant commuting. Respect multilingual and cantonal realities Swiss workplaces often operate across German, French, Italian, and English. A hybrid hub strategy should reflect this reality. Booking instructions, workplace etiquette, signage, and support information should be easy to understand for local and international users. Age-inclusive communication is also about tone. Avoid assuming that younger staff prefer informality or that older staff resist technology. Instead, communicate options clearly and respectfully. For example, explain how to book a workspace, what equipment is available, how visitors can access the site, and what support exists if plans change. In a country where workplace expectations can vary by region and industry, clarity is a form of inclusion. How HR Leaders Can Build Age-Inclusive Hybrid Policies Age inclusion should not depend on individual managers making ad hoc exceptions. It should be built into hybrid work policy, workspace access, team norms, and performance measurement. For HR leaders, this is an opportunity to make flexible work more consistent and fair. The strongest policies do three things well: they define outcomes, give employees practical choices, and prevent flexibility from turning into isolation. Create choice without creating silos Hybrid work can unintentionally divide teams. Younger employees may come into the office more often for mentoring and visibility. Older employees may choose quieter spaces or remote work to avoid unnecessary travel. Parents may cluster around school schedules. Leaders may default to headquarters, making others feel secondary. To avoid this, companies should design shared rituals that include all age groups: Set team anchor days for activities that genuinely benefit from in-person interaction. Use hubs for mentoring sessions, project kick-offs, and client preparation. Rotate meeting locations when teams are spread across cities or cantons. Make remote participation high quality when attendance is optional. Avoid rewarding presence over contribution. Hybrid hubs work best when they are not treated as overflow offices. They should be part of a deliberate workplace ecosystem that includes home, headquarters, client sites, and on-demand professional spaces. For a broader view of this shift, see Deskimo’s perspective on office-optional workspaces . Set expectations for psychological safety Age inclusion is also cultural. Employees should not feel embarrassed to ask for a quieter room, request larger screen access, choose a workspace nearer home, or decline a late meeting after a long commute. These are not signs of lower commitment. They are practical choices that support sustainable performance. Swiss employers already pay close attention to working conditions, health, and safety. The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs provides guidance on workplace health protection through SECO’s occupational health information . For hybrid teams, the same mindset should extend to distributed workspaces and meeting practices. A psychologically safe hub culture means employees can say what helps them work well. Deskimo’s article on psychosocial safe work hubs explores how workspace decisions influence stress, trust, and team health—issues that matter across age groups. Designing Hubs That Work Across Career Stages A high-performing hybrid hub is not just a desk and Wi-Fi connection. It is a professional environment that supports the full range of work: focus, learning, client service, collaboration, recovery, and transition time between meetings. For Swiss hybrid teams, the best spaces balance efficiency with comfort. They are easy to reach, easy to book, and easy to use. They feel professional enough for client-facing work and calm enough for focused tasks. Facilities that support age inclusion Facilities are often where inclusion becomes visible. Small improvements can reduce fatigue, support concentration, and make people feel welcome. When evaluating coworking spaces, serviced offices, or flexible hubs, look beyond location and price. Use this checklist: Ergonomics: Are chairs adjustable? Are desks comfortable for long sessions? Are external monitors available? Lighting: Is there enough natural light? Are work areas free from glare and harsh brightness? Acoustics: Are there quiet zones, phone rooms, and meeting rooms with good sound insulation? Accessibility: Are entrances, lifts, toilets, and corridors suitable for people with mobility needs? Booking simplicity: Can employees reserve space quickly without complex approvals? Privacy: Are there options for sensitive HR, legal, finance, or client conversations? Refreshment and breaks: Are there comfortable areas to pause between calls? Transport access: Is the hub close to train, tram, bus, or parking options? These factors are not only relevant to older employees. They support every professional who has ever had back-to-back video calls, carried equipment across town, or needed a quiet place before a client presentation. Programming that brings generations together Workplace design is not only physical. Programming matters too. Hybrid hubs can create valuable moments for cross-generational learning without making them feel forced. Examples include: Mentoring mornings where early-career employees can book time with senior specialists. Reverse mentoring sessions focused on digital tools, social platforms, or emerging work habits. Project clinics where mixed-age teams solve client or operational challenges. Leadership drop-in hours at regional hubs rather than only headquarters. Skills exchanges across language regions, such as German-speaking and French-speaking teams sharing market knowledge. These activities help reduce stereotypes. Younger employees gain context and judgement from experienced colleagues. Older employees stay close to new tools, customer behaviours, and emerging expectations. Everyone benefits from stronger internal networks. Using Data to Improve Hybrid Hubs Without Losing Trust Age-inclusive hybrid work should be evidence-based. Otherwise, companies risk making decisions based on assumptions: that older workers prefer home, younger workers prefer buzz, or managers need the office more than specialists. Data can challenge these assumptions, but it must be used carefully. The goal is not to monitor individuals. The goal is to understand patterns so that companies can provide the right mix of spaces in the right locations. Measure patterns, not personalities Workspace data can show which hubs are used, when demand peaks, what room sizes are needed, and whether teams are travelling farther than necessary. This helps companies adjust budgets and improve employee experience. Useful metrics include: Hub usage by location and day of week. Meeting room demand versus individual desk demand. Average commute distance to selected workspaces. No-show rates and booking changes. Employee feedback on noise, comfort, and accessibility. Use of spaces for mentoring, client meetings, or team workshops. Data becomes more inclusive when paired with listening. For example, if a suburban hub is popular with employees over 50, do not assume they are disengaging from the office. Ask what works: shorter commutes, quieter rooms, easier parking, or better focus time. Those insights may help younger employees too. For practical ideas on using workplace data responsibly, Deskimo’s guide to badge data for smarter hybrid space planning shows how usage signals can support better real estate decisions. Turn feedback into visible improvements Employees are more likely to share honest feedback when they see action. If people report that a hub is too noisy, add quiet zones or offer alternatives. If booking is confusing, simplify the flow. If older employees avoid certain locations because of poor lighting or uncomfortable seating, address the basics before launching a new engagement campaign. Age inclusion improves when organisations treat feedback as operational intelligence rather than a complaint channel. In Switzerland’s high-trust professional culture, this matters. Employees expect quality, reliability, and follow-through. A Better Hybrid Model for Every Career Stage Age-inclusive hubs help Swiss organisations turn hybrid work from a scheduling arrangement into a competitive advantage. They reduce commute pressure, support longer and more flexible careers, improve collaboration across generations, and make professional workspaces available where people need them most. The key is to design for real life. Teams are not made up of identical workers with identical needs. They include new joiners building confidence, parents balancing responsibilities, experts protecting focus time, leaders meeting clients, and experienced professionals sharing knowledge across the business. For HR leaders, entrepreneurs, freelancers, and remote workers in Switzerland, age inclusion is a practical lens for better workspace decisions. Choose hubs that are accessible, quiet when needed, easy to book, technologically reliable, and welcoming across career stages. Then support those spaces with clear policies, respectful communication, and data-informed improvements. When hybrid work is designed this way, everyone gains: employees feel trusted, companies use space more intelligently, and teams stay connected without unnecessary friction. title: PPPS Week: Honoring Community Supervision Professionals
summary: Every day, more than 90,000 community supervision professionals help make our communities safer and create opportunities for lasting change. And each July, those contributions are recognized by the American Probation and Parole Association (APPA) during Pretrial, Probation, and...
body_text: PPPS Week: Honoring Community Supervision Professionals July 23, 2026 by Ashlin McMaken Every day, more than 90,000 community supervision professionals help make our communities safer and create opportunities for lasting change. Whether they are supervising individuals, coordinating with courts and service providers, or helping people navigate reentry, community supervision professionals are a critical piece of the justice ecosystem. And each July, those contributions are recognized by the American Probation and Parole Association (APPA) during Pretrial, Probation, and Parole Supervision (PPPS) Week . What was once a single state proclamation has since grown into a nationwide tradition of celebrating those whose mission is to protect public safety and create continuity from custody to community. This year’s theme, “ Connected for Change: Building Bridges in Supervision ,” highlights a reality supervision officers know well: meaningful outcomes depend on meaningful connections. APPA Executive Director Veronica Ballard Cunningham described it as “officers are bridge builders of justice” — professionals who help individuals meet supervision requirements, find services, and build a path toward better outcomes. This work creates opportunities for lasting change. Learning From Community Supervision Agencies in the Field APPA marked PPPS Week with a national tour, visiting professionals across the country to not only show appreciation for those working on the front lines, but to also learn from those developing new approaches to long-standing challenges. Joining APPA on their visits were members of the Tyler Technologies Courts & Justice Division. Their goal was to celebrate the work being done across the country, listen to the challenges of today, and gain a deeper understanding of ideas shaping the future. The Tyler team included: Jack Martin , former director of the Clark County Department of Juvenile Justice Services and current client executive, bringing more than 30 years of experience working with individuals seeking a second chance Larry Stanton , co-founder of Enterprise Supervision (formerly known as CaseloadPRO) with more than 20 years of experience designing and deploying supervision software The team stopped by the annual RISE26 Conference , which focuses on expanding treatment and recovery to justice-involved individuals. Conversations focused on: Where and how officers need more support How agencies are balancing workloads, public safety responsibilities, and rehabilitative goals Which programs and partnerships are making a measurable difference Giving Officers Their Time Back One of the strongest themes to emerge from conversations at RISE was the growing pressure on officers’ time. Agency leaders and practitioners described balancing growing caseloads, strict reporting requirements, and workforce constraints while continuing to deliver meaningful supervision and support. While approaches vary across jurisdictions, leaders in Ohio discussed artificial intelligence (AI) as one potential tool to reclaim an officer’s time spent on reporting, case notes, and documentation. This reflects a broader sentiment across agencies. “Time is an officer’s most valuable resource,” said Martin. “Giving them time back means giving them more opportunities to focus on the people they’re serving.” It’s also a reminder that AI is a tool meant to support — not replace — the human-centered nature that is critical to effective supervision. A common thread present in conversations between supervision professionals was the importance of connection across the supervision ecosystem. Whether they were discussing reporting requirements, technology, or treatment programs, the industry is hungry for stronger information sharing and deeper collaboration that improve outcomes. As the conference suggests, strong partnerships across the supervision continuum — treatment, behavioral health, community services — are essential to bridging the gaps that can exist between corrections, supervision, and successful reentry. How Tyler Supports Supervision Professionals Conversations during PPPS Week were a steady reminder of our mission: to make technology work for you, so you can work for people. Our goal is to work alongside agencies to eliminate friction in their daily work, improve access to information, and strengthen collaboration across the supervision life cycle. Across the country, agencies are already reducing administrative burdens and making data-informed decisions that directly impact the people they serve. Placer County Probation Department, California, and El Paso County Pretrial Department, Texas, are two examples of how that work is taking shape. Placer County is building a more sustainable probation model that allows officers to spend more time in the field and less time behind a desk. They are carefully introducing a responsible AI framework into existing probation practices to alleviate growing caseloads and reporting expectations. Their focus on preserving human-in-the-loop principles will shape how AI should work for probation, not how probation should work for AI. El Paso County is strengthening pretrial client outcomes by connecting data and delivering a more holistic approach to supervision. They’ve eliminated errors and paper pretrial workflows with electronic assessments and automated forms, streamlining how information is shared between justice partners. The result is a more connected continuum of care that helps officers, judges, and practitioners make more informed decisions as they support individuals on their reentry journey. Stronger Connection Drives Meaningful Outcomes Behind meaningful community supervision are the professionals who build stronger connections every day. Connections between officers and clients. Between courts and treatment providers. Between agencies and community partners. These connections help agencies respond more effectively to community needs and create opportunities for improved stability. Together with APPA and the professionals who serve our communities every day, Tyler is committed to supporting a more connected ecosystem for community supervision. body_text: Onde o profissional formado em Administração pode trabalhar? Uma das principais vantagens da graduação em Administração é a versatilidade. O administrador pode atuar em empresas de diferentes portes e segmentos , órgãos públicos, organizações sem fins lucrativos ou até abrir o próprio negócio. Entre as principais áreas de atuação estão: Finanças e Controladoria : planejamento financeiro, orçamento, investimentos e análise de custos. Recursos Humanos (RH) : recrutamento, seleção, treinamento, desenvolvimento de pessoas e gestão de equipes. Marketing e Vendas: planejamento estratégico, relacionamento com clientes, gestão de marcas e campanhas comerciais. Logística e Operações: gestão de estoques, compras, cadeia de suprimentos e distribuição. Consultoria Empresarial : diagnóstico de processos, melhoria da gestão e planejamento estratégico. Empreendedorismo : criação e administração do próprio negócio. Gestão Pública : atuação em órgãos governamentais, autarquias e empresas públicas, geralmente por meio de concursos. Após concluir a graduação, o profissional também pode solicitar registro no Conselho Regional de Administração (CRA) , requisito para o exercício de diversas atividades privativas da profissão.
